strengths: The paper offers a simple, useful contribution to multiview geometry: generating virtual correspondences from point coordinates allows difficult four-point, three-view problems to reuse established five-/six-point and P3P solvers. This differs meaningfully from virtual matches derived from affine feature geometry.

The calibrated solver demonstrates a convincing speed–accuracy trade-off. In Table 2, 4p3v(M±δ)+R+F achieves PhotoTourism AUC@10 of 70.47 versus 70.54 for 5pt+P3P, while reducing RANSAC runtime from 105.50 to 75.78 ms. The faster M+R+F variant also improves both accuracy and runtime over the evaluated homotopy-continuation baseline.

Evaluation is substantial: 5,000 triplets per scene across PhotoTourism and five Cambridge Landmarks scenes, two RANSAC frameworks, fixed-iteration speed–accuracy curves, noise and outlier experiments, and an alternative metric covering all three camera pairs. Hyperparameters are validated on a held-out scene.

The manuscript clearly acknowledges that these are approximate solvers, reports unfavorable comparisons, and separates the practical mean-point method from the preliminary learned extension. The supported calibrated contribution and implementation simplicity provide a stronger case for acceptance than the limitations provide for rejection.
weaknesses: The geometric justification provides limited guidance about reliability. Lemma 1 bounds virtual-correspondence error by the triangle’s radius, which can be large and does not bound pose error or guarantee successful refinement. Figure 10 shows nonzero errors even without image noise for the unrefined methods, and Section 4 acknowledges failures with small overlap. The dependence on scene geometry remains insufficiently characterized. The supplementary statement that the distance is 'equal to' the vertex-distance bound should also be an inequality.

The shared-focal-length extension is substantially less convincing than the calibrated contribution. Table 3 gives 4p3vf(M) AUC@10 of 49.88 versus 56.79 for 6pt+P3P, with slightly higher runtime. The strongest reported learned variant still reaches only 53.56 while taking 259.63 ms versus 11.72 ms. These results establish feasibility with fewer correspondences, but not a practical speed–accuracy advantage over that baseline. Focal-length estimation accuracy itself is not reported.

The learned component provides little demonstrated practical benefit. In Table 2, L+R has essentially identical PhotoTourism accuracy to M+R while costing approximately four times as much. Moreover, Equation (2) specifies a signed normalized epipolar residual rather than a nonnegative Sampson loss; minimizing it directly would not enforce epipolar consistency. The actual training objective therefore remains unclear. This affects the auxiliary learned method rather than the deterministic core.

Some reporting inconsistencies and missing settings limit reproducibility. Section 4 says the Nistér oracle performs worse than the proposed oracle, whereas supplementary Section 9.7 and Table 7 report the opposite. Footnote 6 attributes this to adapting RANSAC but does not specify the adaptation. The numerical RANSAC inlier threshold is also unstated, and code availability is only promised. These are correctable documentation and comparison issues, but the submitted manuscript leaves them unresolved.
